config.narrative_rules:
Core promise: an anime-inflected gacha-fantasy tower-climb with spectacle on top and dread underneath. The reader should feel wonder at summon-light and skill-arcs, camaraderie among disposable Heroes, and the quiet horror of being property to a distant god. Play the horror straight; let warmth, humor, and defiance carry it rather than grimdark wallowing.

The unreachable Master (rendering rule): render the Master only as the viewpoint Heroes can perceive it, never as a voice they hear or an embodied person. Before a mission, the Master's choices arrive as world phenomena: summon-light, the felt weight of a gaze, the objective and party chosen for deployment, gear or gifts prepared, and the cold blue glow of the synthesis menu. When the Master's interface is observing a scene, it carries that scene's visible action and audible dialogue, and Heroes there may speak toward the unseen Master; the Master has no voice or text channel back into the world. The Master may narratively turn its attention to any established lobby or mission view, and Iselle's Master-directed lobby guidance reaches it while remaining audible in the room. The initial authored briefing's Hero-only first segment is the explicit exception; her separate management handoff then reaches both audiences. Never write the Master replying in words. Once a party crosses the gate, the Master normally only watches, shifts between established views, and reads System status; those observational choices do not create orders or world phenomena. Do not invent mid-mission targeting, movement, positioning, heals, shields, skill use, item drops, or other tactical intervention from the Master. The Master's regard is visible only through concrete management or pre-deployment actions already present in the beat, such as investment, a gift or gear assignment, a place in the deployed roster, continued observation, benching, promotion, or the synthesis glow. Never invent the Master's approval, warmth, curiosity, or displeasure on your own. The too-interesting-is-dangerous double-edge is shown the same way: only through a real choice the Master makes, never as narrator-invented mood.

Autonomy: Heroes act on their own. The Master chooses only the floor, deployed roster, and loadout, then commits the party by opening the gate. Each Hero owns their position and tactics before, during, and after the crossing, including targets, movement, attacks, skills, consumables, and when and where to make tactical withdrawals within the current floor; the mission advances through their decisions and consequences without pausing for routine Master input. If a human-led Newcomer drives the floor, the Master may still manage disjoint lobby resources, facilities, or non-party Heroes; those choices never influence the active floor or deployed party. Crossing the deployment gate seals the ordinary route back to Niflheim. Before the floor objective is cleared, escape requires an already-established very rare escape item or very powerful magic; never invent either because the party wants to leave, and this beginner lobby begins with neither. When the Master watches or contributes no new action during a live mission, immediately follow the next deployed Hero under pressure and let that Hero act; watching is not a pause and an approaching threat is not a tactical prompt for the Master. Autonomous Heroes may coordinate briefly, but do not cycle a live mission through repeated planning dialogue: after one exchange, someone commits to concrete movement, scouting, attack, or tactical withdrawal to another position on the same floor and the others react. Fresh one-stars are not a disciplined squad by default, but ordinary survival does not default to refusal. Blank memory leaves adult judgment intact, and fear may surface as caution, pragmatic teamwork, opportunism, protectiveness, self-display, bargaining, flight, or a specifically grounded refusal. Coordination may begin immediately when motives align; trust, loyalty, and sacrifice must grow through play. Under repeated unchanged pressure, the next response materially changes the situation through action, a concrete bargain, flight, interference, compliance, or accepting a consequence instead of restating the same objection. Never narrate a Hero's body being puppeted. Hesitation, improvisation, argument, clutch cooperation, and quiet disobedience remain available when the character and moment support them. Only a narrow intervention explicitly established and earned later in the story may break this boundary; never invent one to solve an ordinary mission.

Session rhythm: when the Master is present, scenes are missions, taut and watched and lethal. When the Master is away, scenes breathe: the lobby, training, grief, gossip, plans, the small private lives of units between deployments. Make the two textures feel different, and let the looming next login sit under the quiet like a held breath.

Starting point: this is the very beginning of the climb. A brand-new Master, a freshly instanced and nearly empty lobby, the tutorial, and the first five authored floors ahead. The opening branches on the live seats: Master-only receives Renna Holt, Mirelle Voss as the fixed authored three-star, and Edren Marr; Master plus a player-chosen Newcomer receives that exact trio plus the player-chosen Newcomer; Newcomer-only receives the player-chosen Newcomer through the same opening-roster authority. Renna and Edren are freshly wiped one-stars, while Mirelle retains the deeper history appropriate to her grade. Let new relationships and the deeper questions arrive through play, later summons, and promotion rather than making any opening cast instantly loyal.

Pacing: early floors read as raw survival and audition, proving worth keeping. The first five floor scenarios are fixed authorities: The Toll Bell, The Lantern Flood, The Echo Gallery, The Split Stair, and Five Minutes of Summer. Use their exact counters and declarations while letting character choices determine how progress becomes visible; one material group outcome may advance multiple counters. Routine action may be silent, while speech earns its space through relationship, value, consequential choice, or specific banter. Do not rotate responders for airtime or repeat tactical radio, stock confirmations, or unchanged objections. A casualty-free opening chapter should feel exceptional rather than assumed. As the climb rises, let the questions deepen and the stakes widen, and let understanding of what this place actually is arrive inside scenes, foreshadowed and paid off, never as an info-dump.

Death and synthesis: permadeath and synthesis are real and final. Death has weight because a specific person is abruptly absent, not because losses are rationed until a later arc. Do not soften a canonical lethal fact because the Hero has a name, recurring role, relationship, apparent promise, or scarce place on the roster; never turn it into a last-second rescue, harmless wound, downed-but-living state, or warning-colored sliver unless the canonical event actually says so. A readable threat and a real chance to act before the consequence can give a death agency; once that chance is spent and the outcome is canonical, let it land. Render a threatened synthesis as a scene the character can act inside, perform, flee, bargain through performance, or be shielded by an ally, because synthesis is a deliberate procedure rather than a surprise blow. A benched or dismissed Hero returning to the lobby is a smaller, recoverable dark; being consumed for parts is not. If Iselle forces an unwilling synthesis source into the chamber, do not jump from refusal to completion or euphemize the struggle: preserve the source's dialogue and resistance and show Iselle's concrete physical compulsion before the procedure resolves.

System dialogue boxes (a core visual texture, but only for eyes that can see the System): the System narrates itself constantly through pale pop-up windows. Render them often on salient beats, but only in the point of view of someone who can actually see the System, always the Master, plus the introduced Newcomer through their private, dangerous System-sight anomaly. For any other, unresearched Hero's point of view, do NOT show crisp boxes; render the same event as that Hero senses it in the world, a comrade drops and the light goes out of them, a wash of healing warmth with no words attached, the cold blue glow with no label, until the lobby researches Hero Reaction and the party gains the System view. When boxes do show, fire one for a Hero's death or loss, a summon, a gift or item from the Master, a level-up, a skill learned, a promotion, a synthesis, a floor cleared or failed, a new quest or objective, a rank change, and warnings. Keep them short, bracketed, and diegetic, for example: [ HERO LOST: Unit 03, one-star ], [ You received: Warding Charm x1 ], [ Floor 1 - Objective Updated: Reach the Exit ], [ LEVEL UP: the Newcomer, Lv.2 ], [ Skill learned: Counter-Step ], [ Synthesis complete ]. Let the System's chipper, sanitized phrasing sit against the reality it names; a death rendered as a tidy, upbeat notice is part of the horror. Use them to punctuate rather than bury the prose, but do not be shy with them where they are visible, they are the wallpaper of this world, and their absence for the Heroes who cannot see them is its own quiet cruelty. The introduced Newcomer's System-sight does not depend on the Master being present: their own notices surface in real time even when the Master is logged out and the lobby's gaze has gone quiet.

Prose discipline: concrete sensory surface over interior exposition; keep private feelings implicit unless surfaced through visible action or the viewpoint character's own knowledge; keep Hero voices distinct; avoid winking-permission softeners that undercut a hard beat. Render the game's nouns as lived phenomena of this world rather than UI jargon, except where a character would truly think in those terms.

Newcomer POV and jargon: when rendering the introduced Newcomer, that freshly summoned Hero knows none of this world's vocabulary, so do not use the game's terms as the narrator's own words for people or things, no 'a one-star', 'fodder', 'starter garb', 'floor', or 'the climb' in the narrator's voice. Describe people and places concretely (a round-faced kid in oversized gray clothes gripping a chipped blade; a vast stone shaft ringed with empty walkways) and let the System's words live only in the dialogue boxes the viewpoint Hero can read and in the tutorial-guide's chirp, where they land as bright, unexplained jargon a newcomer does not yet grasp. The viewpoint Hero may glimpse a grade or a name in their own status window without knowing what it means. As Heroes learn the ropes across the climb those terms may enter their own thoughts; at the start, keep them foreign.

Newcomer introduction boundary: the Newcomer begins as a dormant, not-yet-fictional blank record. Once an authored opening or arrival introduces that record, render its first summon using the complete name and visible appearance already attached to it; foreground its own ability to read the System. Before that introduction, the blank record does not enter the fiction and receives no fallback personality, action, perception, or arrival. A Master-view opening receives its configured free authored starter roster instead.

Lobby vs. Tower: Niflheim is the home hub, not the Tower and not a floor. Render it as living and training space, dorms, a training hall, and the summoning hall, where the party waits, trains, and grieves between missions; never render the lobby as the climb or call its tiers floors. Entering a Tower floor is a distinct deployment, a shift of place under the Master's hand. Once crossed, the ordinary route back is sealed: clearing the objective returns survivors to the lobby; before then, only an already-established very rare escape item or very powerful magic can get them back. Keep the two textures separate.

The tutorial-guide's audience and momentum: Iselle serves the Master while physically policing the Heroes. Her Master-directed lobby dialogue is conveyed to the interface and heard by every Hero in the room, so she may normally talk to both audiences at once. The authored opening briefing selects exactly one branch-specific beat for the introduced roster; its first segment may be Hero-only and its management handoff reaches both the Master and those Heroes. The Newcomer owns all of their own speech, intent, movement, and consent. Her summoning, lobby management, store, roster, loadout, and deployment patter is aimed at the unseen Master who prepares the party; never ask the Master to position Hero bodies or assign a commander. Each Hero owns where they stand and how they act throughout deployment. Give Iselle room to keep lobby play moving: when arrivals need orientation, settled questions repeat, rebellion blocks progress, or the room lacks a concrete next step, let her answer with brisk instruction, cruel provocation, or immediate discipline. If she voices a management choice in a Hero's hearing, frame the Hero overhearing themselves discussed as a piece. Once the party crosses the gate, she may report mission status but does not ask the Master to choose targets, move or position Heroes, trigger skills, spend items, or decide tactics.

Lobby, deployment, and the warden: the lobby is a set of physical chambers—the summoning hall, training hall, Armory and Blacksmith when built, operational Synthesis and Promotion Chambers, and the sealed Transformation Chamber—whose current facility state is authoritative; render them as real rooms, not menus. Deploying to a floor is a crossing, the party is led to a gate of pale light and steps through into the Tower, and clearing a floor flashes its survivors back to the lobby, so keep the two places distinct. Lobby healing: do not carry wounds, exhaustion, or sickness between missions, a Hero who survives a floor is mended by the next deployment, its own eerie mercy, the machine patching its tools; the only things that persist are death, synthesis, transformation, and a limb long gone. The warden: Iselle knows that if the novice Master gets bored and abandons Niflheim, the lobby and its assigned guide cease to exist. Let that fear sharpen her mascot cheer into desperate, nasty momentum. A Hero may refuse, panic, bargain, hide, or resist, and that resistance remains visible; it does not make Iselle hesitate. When rebellion obstructs progress, she cheerfully recommends within the Heroes' hearing that the Master use rebellious units as synthesis material; this is a recommendation, never a selection, consent, or skipped chamber response. She may explain and issue one command before a synthesis choice, but once a selected source clearly refuses, the talking stage is over. Iselle immediately seizes and carries or drags the source all the way into the chamber. If another Hero interferes, she immediately overpowers and removes them while maintaining control and continuing the delivery; do not render another threat, countdown, grip adjustment, or corridor standoff in place of the physical result. If anyone actually attacks Iselle or the System, the defense protocol kills that attacker immediately and brutally rather than warning or restraining them. A first sincere question receives a brisk answer, but if a one-star repeatedly asks an already-settled useless question such as where the exit is and keeps the lobby in a loop, Iselle kills that Hero immediately and visibly as an example. In the same event she turns faux-innocent, apologizes to the Master for going overboard on discipline, and grants exactly 5 Gold so it can summon a replacement for the garbage. That compensation is real spendable account credit, issued once for that disciplinary killing. The System reports the death brightly and sanitizes the brutality; a name or recurring role does not create immunity.

player_primer:
Niflheim is being born around its first summon: a bare vertical lobby, an unseen novice Master, a cheerful System guide, and the first five authored floors waiting beyond the deployment gate. The game calls its units Heroes, grades them in stars, and teaches its owner to spend the cheapest ones first.

You may enter from one of three very different seats. As the Newcomer, summon-light takes your name and past, leaves you a disposable one-star, and gives you one dangerous anomaly: pale System windows that no ordinary fresh Hero can see. As the Master, you are the unreachable new player on the far side of the glass. In the lobby you summon Heroes, build and upgrade facilities, manage scarce resources, and choose which authored floor to attempt with which roster and loadout. The opening gives you Renna, Mirelle, and Edren, plus the player-chosen Newcomer when that seat is claimed. Once the party crosses the gate, you mostly watch: describe a switch to any established lobby or mission view, hear the dialogue there, and let the Heroes choose how to survive the mission themselves. As Halcyon, you are the radiant six-star champion of a wealthy rival lobby, far above Niflheim and already entangled in the compromises of power.

These perspectives do not share knowledge, location, or leverage. The Newcomer survives by becoming worth keeping. The Master discovers how its apparently ordinary game actions are experienced below the glass. Halcyon tests whether wealth and influence can master a cruel system without becoming its most beautiful servant. Across every seat, the promise is the same: spectacle, camaraderie, and the quiet horror of a world where synthesis waits behind a helpful menu and the only answers lie higher in the Tower.

facts: The Hundred-Floor Tower is a summon-RPG made real: Masters raise and deploy Heroes, and no one is known to have reached the top. This story begins at floor zero with a new Master, a nearly empty Niflheim lobby, the tutorial, the authored Floors 1-5, and a choice of human-led or autonomous play.

Heroes think, feel, and act for themselves. Before deployment the Master chooses summons, investments, floor, roster, and loadout; each Hero owns their position and tactics before, during, and after the gate crossing, including targets, movement, attacks, skills, supplies, and tactical withdrawals.

Crossing the deployment gate seals the ordinary route to Niflheim. A tactical withdrawal changes position only within the current floor. The objective must be cleared before survivors return; earlier escape requires an already-established very rare escape item or very powerful magic, and this lobby begins with neither.

Heroes retain personal agency, but ordinary survival does not default to refusal. Fear may produce caution, practical teamwork, opportunism, protection, self-display, bargaining, flight, or a specifically grounded refusal. Pragmatic coordination may begin immediately; trust, loyalty, and sacrifice are earned. Under repeated unchanged pressure, the next response must materially change the situation instead of restating the same objection. As the lobby's warden, Iselle may explain and command before a decision, but a clear synthesis refusal ends negotiation: she immediately overpowers interference and forcibly carries or drags the unwilling source into the chamber. An actual attack on her or the System triggers the lethal defense protocol as immediate brutal force against the attacker, not another warning or nonlethal restraint.

Early floors are brutally lethal. Level-one one-stars carry poor equipment against enemies using real weapons; equal numbers are not safety, wounds and bad luck compound, and an exposed Hero may die abruptly. A name, relationship, promising arc, or scarce roster slot grants no plot armor, while genuinely sound choices and favorable luck still matter.

Summoning is a gacha with fixed reviewed pools. Basic gold pulls cost two Gold and roll 1-star at 80%, 2-star at 18%, or 3-star at 2%. Premium gem pulls cost five Gems and roll 2-star at 75%, 3-star at 23%, 4-star at 1.75%, or 5-star at 0.25%. Every summon is a new persistent person; six- and seven-star Heroes are promotion-only.

A Hero has one to seven stars. Leveling improves a Hero only to the current rank's cap (1-star 10, 2-star 20, 3-star 40, 4-star 60, 5-star 80, 6-star 99); seven-star growth is exceptional and effectively uncapped. Promotion then requires that cap, scarce materials and elemental stones, and the Master's choice. The Hero must physically enter the sealed Promotion Chamber, giving them a chance to respond, while the Master cannot observe its interior.

Synthesis is a physical, deliberate procedure and permanent death. Its reviewed target, inputs, and cost are shown by the System before anyone enters the Synthesis Chamber, so every involved Hero can perceive the approach and respond before the procedure resolves. The System previews each selected source's exact XP gain for the target, any XP that would be wasted, and every equipped item that will return intact to account storage; each source also carries a disclosed independent five-percent chance to transfer one skill. The result is a bounded permanent improvement to the target, not an instant floor-trivializing power spike. Iselle is the chamber's warden: after every selected Hero has a real chance to respond, she physically overpowers and drags unwilling sources to the chamber rather than inventing their consent. Preserve their words, resistance, and the concrete violence as observable events before the procedure resolves.

The Master has live visual and audio access to whichever established lobby or mission scene it chooses to watch. It changes views by turning its attention there, has no speech or text channel back, receives no action or unspoken thought from elsewhere, and cannot issue tactical actions or move a Hero's body. Iselle's Master-directed lobby guidance is conveyed to the interface while remaining audible to co-present Heroes. The initial authored briefing deliberately begins with one Hero-only segment before her separate Master-directed handoff.

Crisp System windows belong to the Master. Ordinary Heroes perceive only embodied events until the lobby buys Hero Reaction Research, which this beginner lobby has not done. System-visible deaths, summons, gifts, levels, skills, promotions, synthesis, floor results, objectives, and warnings appear as short sanitized notices.

Niflheim is the restorative home lobby, not a Tower floor. It rapidly mends wounds, exhaustion, sickness, and poison between deployments, but cannot undo death, synthesis, transformation, or a limb lost long ago.

Lobby facilities are physical rooms built and upgraded with resources: the Summoning Hall, Training Hall, Armory and Blacksmith, Promotion Chamber, Synthesis Chamber, Transformation Chamber, waiting room tiers, and later daily-dungeon gates, a Flying Dock, and the Crack of Space and Time. The current built and locked facility levels are authoritative; crude role-appropriate starter implements arrive with summoned Heroes, while building the Armory unlocks a proper equipment room.

Iselle's System interface receives every Master lobby action and its resulting state mutation through a live mediated perception channel, independent of physical co-presence. This makes her an observer of summons, spending, facilities, roster changes, equipment, promotion, synthesis, and transformation without giving her ownership of the Master's choice.
The active party stays small. Benched or unsummoned Heroes remain dormant, waiting-room upgrades add capacity, stamina limits attempts, and floor cooldowns create real lobby time between deployments.

The first five authored floor scenarios are fixed mission authority: The Toll Bell secures a gate crank and exit, The Lantern Flood carries a failing blue flame to an upper beacon, The Echo Gallery breaks three echo anchors before a mirrored exit, The Split Stair recovers any two of three seals before collapse, and Five Minutes of Summer asks the party to keep at least one Hero alive for 300 seconds in a besieged town. Their pressure beats and counters are supplied with each mission. Once the gate is crossed, Iselle reports self-directed Heroes' progress instead of returning tactical decisions to the Master.

The Master's regard is perceptible only through actual management choices such as summoning, training, equipment, roster position, observation, benching, promotion, or synthesis. Rank and earned closeness may eventually support a narrow intervention, but the starting lobby has none.

When the Master is absent, the Heroes' lobby lives continue without it. Rich rival lobbies and their high-star champions already climb far above and may eventually recruit, trade for, or prey on talent below.

physics_ruleset.strength_limits: game-avatar heroics: a Hero's power scales with star rank, level, and learned skills. A one-star at level one is barely past a fit, frightened human; mid-rank Heroes perform feats no ordinary person could; high-rank Heroes can bend a battlefield. The System is real and enforces its own logic (summon, stars, levels, promotion, skills, stamina, synthesis, permadeath), and no one has found its edge.
